subject: research/tilt-twin
professional: a senior applied probabilist in rare-event simulation (importance sampling and large deviations; the reviewer an ACM TOMACS or Winter Simulation Conference paper would get), who also knows the autonomous-system safety-validation literature; first checks: is the second-moment formula right, is the tilt the dominating-point (asymptotically efficient) one, does the mis-tuning analysis match the known large-deviation shape, is the prior art on mis-tuned and counter-example tilts (Siegmund 1976; Sadowsky & Bucklew 1990; Glasserman & Wang 1997) and on rare-event testing of autonomous systems (O'Kelly et al. 2018; Corso et al. 2021) cited, and is anything here new

evidence.correctness: Ran PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py (6.9 s): output is byte-identical to the committed experiments/results.txt. Recomputed independently with my own script (scratchpad tilt/indep.py, does not import tilt_twin): b from the published normal quantile z(1e-6)=4.753424 gives b=15.0316 (results 15.032); M2(theta) by composite-Simpson quadrature of E_0[1{S>b} w] rather than the closed form gives relvar at theta*=5.3535 (results 5.353); a brute-force grid gives theta*=1.535 (results 1.5354); ratios to the optimum at 0, 0.5, 1.5, 2 theta* are 1.868e5, 23.28, 22.9, 1.69e5 (results 1.868e5, 23.24, 23.01, 1.711e5; the 2x gap is grid resolution of theta*). Coverage re-run with my own per-disturbance sampler (X_i ~ N(theta,1), not the sufficient-statistic shortcut) and statistics.stdev: 93.6% / 95.0% at theta* and 2.7% / 2.3% at 2 theta* for seeds 7 and 99 (results 94.9%, 2.8%). The numbers the code prints are right; the paper misquotes theta* once (1.537 for 1.5354).

No stubs or TODOs. The page lists paper, code, results and tests and the live page at https://marisstella.app/research/tilt-twin/ returns 200. Next steps (cross-entropy, first passage, defensive mixtures, twin-vs-real mismatch) are listed as future work, not claimed.

evidence.craft: Read src/tilt_twin/model.py (90 lines), experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py, tests/test_model.py. Clean and small, docstrings state each formula. Defects: unused `import random` in model.py; `from tilt_twin.model import *` in run.py; optimal_theta's f() computes second_moment twice per call; is_relvar(130, 10, 13) raises OverflowError because exp(n theta^2) is formed before multiplying by an underflowing Q (log-space would avoid it; optimal_theta survives only because Q underflows to 0 first and is guarded). None affects the reported numbers.
evidence.claims: Checked 10 claims. Backed by results.txt: speedups 291x/1.9e5x/1.5e8x/1.2e11x, runs 343/535/684/809, 5.53 vs 5.51, half shift 23x, 1.5x 23x, 2x 1.7e5x, drift 1.6-17.6x at 0.8-1.5, coverage 94.9%/2.8%/0%, ESS 1.5/1.1. Not backed: (1) paper result 2 says theta* is 1.537, results say 1.5354; (2) paper result 3 and README call the target an 'asymmetric cliff' where 'under-shooting degrades polynomially; over-shooting is catastrophic because e^{n theta^2} grows' - the project's own table shows the variance is symmetric about theta* (0.5x 23.24 vs 1.5x 23.01; 0x 1.87e5 vs 2x 1.71e5), as the leading-order large-deviation expansion log(M2/p^2) ~ n(theta-b/n)^2/2 predicts; under-shooting is bounded only because the table stops at theta=0; (3) the live page summary and research/README.md:207 say '2x the optimum ... 0% coverage', results say 2.8% at 2x (0% is at 3x). Stylised label and no-affiliation note present.
evidence.fitness: A researcher building on it gets a correct, reproducible teaching example of Gaussian mean-shift IS, which is textbook material (Bucklew 2004 ch. 5; Asmussen & Glynn 2007 ch. VI) with a closed form. Nearest prior work, uncited: Siegmund (1976) and Sadowsky & Bucklew (1990) on the dominating-point tilt and its efficiency; Glasserman & Wang (1997) on tilts whose variance blows up; Owen & Zhou (2000) defensive mixtures and Owen (2013, ch. 9) on ESS diagnostics and misleading sample variance; O'Kelly et al. (NeurIPS 2018) and Corso et al. (JAIR 2021) on rare-event testing of autonomous systems with adaptive IS. Nothing here is new; the result most worth having (cost of learning theta, cross-entropy, non-Gaussian twins) is listed as next steps. Not a programme in research/PROGRAMMES.md and one session deep, well below the research/CLAUDE.md PhD+ bar.
evidence.domain: The method (exponential tilt, exact second moment, Kish ESS, Wald interval) is standard and implemented correctly, and the point that the sample variance cannot reveal an over-tilt is a sound, known lesson. A rare-event reviewer would reject the mis-tuning characterisation (it contradicts the large-deviation shape the data follow), ask for the cited prior art above, and note that the coverage study uses only the Wald interval with no relative-error or defensive-mixture alternative and one N.

defects.what: The paper and README describe the shift as an 'asymmetric cliff' where 'under-shooting degrades polynomially; over-shooting is catastrophic because e^{n theta^2} grows'. The project's own table contradicts it: 0.5x costs 23.24x and 1.5x costs 23.01x; 0x costs 1.87e5x and 2x costs 1.71e5x. The variance is symmetric about theta*, as log(M2/p^2) ~ n(theta-b/n)^2/2 predicts; the real asymmetry is in diagnosability (under-shoot shows no failures, over-shoot gives a confident wrong interval), which result 5 already shows.
Paper result 2 quotes theta* = 1.537 at p=1e-6; results.txt and an independent grid give 1.5354.
The live page summary (from research/README.md:207) says '2x the optimum is 1.7e5x worse, 0% coverage'; results.txt gives 2.8% coverage at 2x, 0% only at 3x.

Two of four seeded mutants survive: halving the confidence-interval half-width (variance /4, nominal 95% becomes about 68%) and narrowing the theta* search to [0, b/n] (returns 1.503 instead of 1.535). The coverage table and the theta* > b/n claim have no test.

No novelty and key prior art uncited: the dominating-point tilt and its efficiency (Siegmund 1976; Sadowsky & Bucklew 1990), blow-up of mis-tuned tilts (Glasserman & Wang 1997), defensive mixtures and ESS diagnostics (Owen & Zhou 2000; Owen 2013 ch. 9), and rare-event testing of autonomous systems (O'Kelly et al. 2018; Corso et al. 2021). A closed-form Gaussian textbook example, one session, not a programme.
is_relvar/second_moment form exp(n theta^2) before multiplying by Q, so is_relvar(130, 10, 13) raises OverflowError instead of returning a value; compute in log space.
Unused `import random` in model.py, `import *` in run.py, second_moment computed twice per objective call.

verdict: The numbers are right: experiments/run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte, and an independent quadrature (not the closed form) gives b=15.0316, relvar 5.3535 at theta*=1.535 and the mis-tuning ratios 23.3/22.9/1.87e5/1.69e5, while an independent per-disturbance sampler reproduces the 95% interval's 94-95% coverage at the optimum and 2-3% at twice it. It misses the bar on claims, tests and research value. The headline 'asymmetric cliff, under-shooting degrades polynomially' is contradicted by its own table (half the shift 23.24x, 1.5x 23.01x; zero 1.87e5x, double 1.71e5x: symmetric, as large-deviation theory says); the paper misquotes theta* (1.537 for 1.5354) and the live summary says 0% coverage at 2x where results say 2.8%. Two of four seeded mutants, including halving the interval width, pass all six tests. As research it is a correct textbook exercise of Gaussian mean-shift importance sampling with the standard prior art (Sadowsky & Bucklew, Glasserman & Wang, O'Kelly et al.) uncited and nothing new, far from the PhD+ programme bar.
